issues.legal_issue: A statutory charge in favour of a purchaser requires a genuine agreement to sell immovable property, and a charge cannot take priority if no such statutory charge arose.
material_facts: The competing creditor had advanced money to the property owner, received a promissory note, and obtained an award decree that charged the properties and required a sale of one property if the debt was not paid.

The claimed sale agreement stated that a substantial earnest payment had been made, but the claimant gave inconsistent accounts of that payment and did not produce the original account books or reliable proof of payment.
The terms and surrounding circumstances of the claimed sale, including the absence of meaningful title and property inquiries, did not support a genuine intention to purchase the property.
The Court accepted that the award decree and the underlying creditor transaction were genuine and that the creditor had no notice of the claimed sale agreement.
issues.conclusion: The claimed transaction was not a genuine agreement to sell immovable property and therefore did not create a statutory charge under Section 55(6)(b) of the Transfer of Property Act. The claimant had no charge that could take priority over the charge under the award decree, so the High Court’s priority finding was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Section 55(6)(b) of the Transfer of Property Act gives a purchaser a charge in specified circumstances for purchase money paid under a contract of sale, but the provision applies only where there is a genuine agreement to sell immovable property. Without that statutory charge, there can be no priority based on it. The judgment relies on no earlier cases.

predicates.competing_property_charge_claims: The proceeding concerns competing claims to a charge over the same property.
predicates.purchaser_claims_statutory_charge: A person claiming to be a purchaser seeks a statutory charge based on an alleged agreement to sell the property.
predicates.alleged_sale_is_not_genuine: The alleged agreement does not represent a genuine transaction for the sale of the property.
predicates.purchaser_has_no_statutory_charge_or_pri: The claimed purchaser has neither the statutory charge nor priority based on that charge.

issues.definition: When competing claims to a property charge include a purchaser’s claim based on an alleged sale that is not genuine, the purchaser has no statutory charge or priority.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court cannot rely on account books that were not proved at trial when doing so deprives the opposing party of an opportunity to challenge the material.
material_facts: The claimant relied at trial on extracts that he said he had prepared from his account books, but the original books were not produced and the extracts were not shown to have been verified against them.
The extracts were not established as admissible evidence at trial.

On appeal, the High Court inspected the original books and relied on them to find that the claimed earnest money had been paid, without giving the opposing party an opportunity to cross-examine the claimant about the books or their entries.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in inspecting and relying on the books of account in those circumstances; the books had not been proved at trial and the extracts were inadmissible.
issues.legal_principle: Account books that have not been proved in evidence cannot be used to establish the asserted transactions merely because an appellate court later inspects them. Where material is considered without the opposing party having an opportunity to challenge it through cross-examination, the appellate court cannot rely on it to determine the issue. The judgment cites no statutory provision or earlier case for this principle.

predicates.appeal_from_trial_decision: The matter is an appeal from a decision made after a trial.
predicates.account_books_not_proved_at_trial: A party did not prove the account books at trial, and any extracts were not established as admissible evidence.
predicates.appellate_court_relies_on_books_without_: The appellate court relies on the books without allowing the opposing party an opportunity to challenge them.
predicates.appellate_court_must_not_rely_on_unprove: The appellate court must not rely on the unproved books to decide the issue.

issues.definition: In an appeal from a trial decision, an appellate court must not rely on account books that were unproved at trial when the opposing party had no opportunity to challenge them.
